P01.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations had no reporters and read the papers' stories aloud only after the morning papers were on the street. Advertisers moved their money to the stations, which undercut the single rate the papers set together, and by 1940 most papers had shrunk from twenty-four pages to eight and closed every bureau outside their own city. What room was left went to each city's own courts, council and schools. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In 1952, after three dry years, a river broke its banks and spread for five days across a broad valley, filling every side channel between its villages and their fields. It came down fast off bare slopes carrying coarse gray sand, which it dropped wherever the current slowed: in old stream channels, in ditches and in the low hollows the farmers had always plowed around. The next spring they plowed whole farms in straight furrows for the first time, and the wheat sown in the old hollows came up no thicker than anywhere else. One agronomist later argued that, for the farmers, the flood had above all ______ their fields.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. Rings in its oldest beams date them to the 1490s. Its four shrines stand in the city temple's order, and the dragons over the city temple's gate match its own, scale for scale, at three times the size. Records name the city temple's builder as a carpenter on the hill in his youth. Its farming families still walk to the city each spring for the great festival. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1904 a new firm began making typewriters in a country where one older company had sold nearly every machine for thirty years, and by 1914 the newcomer was outselling it. Its machine, designed from scratch by its own engineers, was judged equal to the older model in trade tests. In 1906 it bound every large dealer in the country, and the only two makers of typewriter ribbon, to contracts forbidding them to handle the older company's goods. Reading both firms' records, one historian concluded that the newcomer had above all ______ its rival.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there is frozen fast to the shore, thick and snow-covered, so the water beneath stays dark and almost nothing grows there. Young cod spend the winter in crevices on its underside, swimming out at night to feed in open water past its edge. The seabirds that hunt them find fish by sight, and at the bay's mouth, where no ice forms, they take most of the young cod wintering there. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1897 gold was found in the hills above a small river town, and the rush lasted six years. In its first summer some nine thousand miners came up the river road, a dozen for every resident, and camped in the churchyard and along the main street until the town council stopped meeting. When the gold gave out in 1903 they left as fast as they had come. By 1920 the town again had about eight hundred people, the same families farming the same fields, its main street still facing the river landing. Looking back in 1920, one historian wrote that the gold rush had ______ the town.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: Between the two world wars, exiles working for their small homeland's independence gathered at a café in a foreign capital, where the owner kept the back room for them. The movement's leaders lived in hiding at home and sent word only of what the café should tell its visitors. Five exiles chosen for their command of the capital's language sat at the long table, and foreign reporters, diplomats and members of parliament came there to hear the homeland's case before every debate on it. In a memoir of those years, one journalist called the café, more than anything, the movement's ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. By 1500 one family in the coastal city had bought every palm and well, and its stewards had the dates harvested by tenants and carried to the coast on the family's own camels. Caravans watered there free, all year, and could buy nothing there, since every date was spoken for. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. In the village versions recorded around 1900, all eleven episodes remained, taking as long to tell as the printed text took to read. The desert capital had become the valley's market town, the robber king a lord from the next valley and the son's camel a mule, and each teller's wording differed from every other's. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1590 the council of a river city built a stone granary on its market square, large enough to hold a year's grain for every household. The city's own bread came from merchants at prices that rose and fell with each harvest. Whenever a village lord within a day's ride refused the city's toll on river barges, the council sent buyers to that village's market, who filled the granary with every sack on sale there at any price. No lord held out past the next sowing. One economic historian has argued that for two centuries the granary served above all as the city's ______.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: A chalk quarry worked out in the 1800s lies at the edge of a market town, a pit two hundred yards across with galleries cut back into its walls. Its floor is level turf, drained by a tunnel to the river, and on its north side the slope has been cut into grass terraces that face a flat platform of chalk. Each June the town's pageant is played on that platform before most of the town. The galleries were bricked up after a roof fall in 1890. One local historian has called the quarry, above all, the town's ______.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: In 1980 a storm dropped a two-hundred-year-old fir into a mountain stream, and its trunk, four feet thick, has lain there ever since. It came to rest across the stream, its ends on both banks, a few feet above a bedrock chute that runs too deep and fast to wade for a mile in either direction. Trail cameras catch martens, deer mice and bobcats on it every night, and the moss along its top has worn down to a bare strip a foot wide. After a decade of watching it, one ecologist called the log, above all, the valley's ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: A cave opens in the side of a limestone hill above a village, and its passages wind back for a mile under the hill. It has no other opening, and in all weathers a candle flame stands upright in its passages. The drips from its roof collect in a clay-floored basin near the mouth, which rises through the winter and falls slowly through the summer, and in dry years the village carries its water up from there. Its air is the same mild temperature all year. In a survey of the district, one geologist called the cave, above all, the hill's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. Each spring its staff sowed strains sent by breeders in other states in narrow strips beside the district's usual wheat. After five seasons the station printed each strain's harvests in the county paper, and farmers who wanted one of the few strains that had held up ordered its seed from the breeder. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In a pond where half the snails carry a parasitic worm that matures inside ducks, a biologist kept infected and uninfected snails side by side for three years, in tanks and in a pen with feeding ducks. Infected snails grew to half the size of the others and laid a third as many eggs, and they lived just as long. Ducks in the pen took the two kinds at the same rate, and a bacterium that swept the tanks in the second summer killed them at the same rate too. From these results, she concluded that the worm had, above all, ______ its host.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Young stoats dispersing each autumn from farms south of the valley toward the hills to its north reached the hedge at dusk, slept through the following day in old burrows in its bank, and went on north across the fields the next night. No collared stoat was ever trapped in the hedge twice. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. The ore lay in a dozen scattered pockets near the surface, and each was dug out from above as an open pit, some a quarter mile across, the deepest now holding rainwater. Between the pits the slopes keep their old forest, and the summit cairn of 1885 still stands. Trout still rise in the streams that drain the slopes. Surveying the mountain in 1980, one geologist wrote that mining had ______ it.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: From 1950 to 1990, scientists studied one small, deep, cold lake in a northern forest more closely than any other lake in the region, and its bottom mud lies in fine yearly layers. The layers are all the same thickness whatever the weather, one pale band each summer, and scientists elsewhere in the region dated their own lakes' cores by matching shared bands of volcanic ash against its exact count of years. Its shrimp and plankton are those of every lake nearby. In a history of that work, one scientist called the lake, for those four decades, above all the region's ______.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In 1965 a carmaker from abroad opened a plant outside a port city, on a site its board had chosen after two years of study. The company had sold cars in the country through an importer since 1930, and the plant's long sheds now held as many as twenty thousand cars shipped whole from abroad, with spare parts for every model, until dealers across the country called for them. Its one short line only fitted radios, and the company opened no factory there until 1990. In a history of the company, one economist called the plant, above all, its ______ in the country.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. By the eighth week the gauge halfway down read no flow at all, and the gravel riffles between the deep bends lay dry and white. The bends, with no seepage to feed them, sank week by week; biologists who netted their last trout into tanks returned two weeks later to cracked mud. The autumn rains soaked into the bed for two days before any water reached the lake. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Landing twenty years later, surveyors had to dig down through hard gray layers to reach the doorways of the village's houses, which still stood in their rows, and on the slopes only the tops of the orchard walls showed. The harbor lighthouse leaned toward the sea on a cracked base, while every benchmark they dug down to sat at its 1880 height. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, the belt's inner edge stayed sharp for the whole billion years: any icy body that drifted inward toward the giant's orbit was tugged back out within a few thousand circuits, and almost none was lost. Without the giant the belt spread inward into a thin haze, and in both runs the rocky planets were struck about equally often. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: In 1894 a court ruled on a strike by a port city's dockworkers' union, which then had four thousand members and a hall near the docks. The court let the union stand but barred it from enrolling any man hired after the ruling. Its members struck together in 1901 and in 1910 and won both times. As they grew old and retired, no one took their places in the union, and in 1931 its last local closed its doors and sold the hall. Writing fifty years later, one labor historian concluded that the ruling had, in effect, ______ the union.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. X-rays taken in the workshop showed figures beneath the heavy robes of the two saints and beneath the clouds above them. The robes and clouds proved to be paint added in the 1700s and came away with a mild solvent, leaving the original glazes on the faces intact, and the oak panels went back into the frame as they had come out. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. Each winter an ice dam forms at the lake's outlet, and the lake rises fifty feet while the channel below runs nearly dry. When the dam breaks in late spring the stored water pours out within weeks; by July the drained lake is shallow, and its outflow is as warm as the river above, so the ponds turn to wells. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. The road followed the riverbank below the town, on land the railroad had abandoned. Within a decade most of the mill's younger workers had taken jobs in the city, and families drove south on Saturdays to shop. By 1990 the town still had nearly eight thousand people, and eleven of the forty stores on its main street remained. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: A gravel bar a mile long runs from the southern shore of a bay toward an island at the bay's mouth. It ends a quarter mile short of the island in water deep enough for any merchant ship, and ships also pass beyond the island. Winter swells break white along its seaward face. Behind it the town's boats lie at open moorings until spring, while ports elsewhere on that coast haul their fleets ashore from November to March. One historian of the bay's fishing town wrote that the bar had served the town above all as its ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. Crews could no longer hold fish back in their ice holds for a better price, so every fish caught went under the hammer the morning it was landed, while the number of buyers stayed about the same. By 1934 a third of each dawn's catch was going to the fertilizer works at a few cents a crate. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. When the staff returned, the dust on the reading tables lay unbroken, every book stood in its place, the rare-book room included, and the catalog matched the shelves card for card. The occupation's records list the building only as requisitioned, and the city's readers had gone five years without a public library. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. A law of 1850 raised the rate whenever wheat at the capital's exchange fell below one price and cut it whenever wheat rose above another, and all eleven changes, five of them cuts, followed that law under whichever party governed. Over the century, wheat prices there moved half as much as in the neighboring countries, whose duties were set by their own parliaments' votes. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: A cave high in a cliff overlooks a ford where reindeer herds crossed a river each spring and autumn fourteen thousand years ago; its back chamber stays near freezing all year. At the cave's mouth stands a waist-high wall of stacked stones facing the ford, and behind it excavators found small hearths, broken spear tips and flakes from making new ones, all from the weeks when herds were crossing. The reindeer bones of those weeks lay butchered and burned in a riverside camp, beside grass bedding and children's milk teeth. From the finds, one archaeologist concluded that the valley's hunters used the cave above all as their ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: Between 1925 and 1935 a record company sent engineers into a mountain region to record its fiddlers and ballad singers, and it sold the records by the thousand. Most of the records sold in mill cities two hundred miles east, where families from the mountains had gone for work, and their children, learning from the records, formed string bands that played the ballads whole and in the old rough style. In the region itself the songs faded within a generation, as the singers themselves followed the mills east. Looking back in 1970, one folklorist argued that the records had ______ the region's songs.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water, clear snowmelt that had crossed the upland meadows, stood nine days and sank through the sandy ground into the ditches below. Last year's stubble still stood, and the fallow strips along the ditches came up as bare as ever. That summer the same seed wheat that had always yielded half as much there as on the upper slopes matched them. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: A sand spit four miles long curves across a lagoon's mouth, with a lighthouse near its hooked tip and a road along its crest. In 1953 a three-day gale drove waves over the crest. Afterward the spit was as wide as before, and the keeper drove the crest road to the lighthouse. The light, which had stood four hundred yards back from the tip, now stood at the water's edge, and the lagoon's mouth had widened by as much. Ordinary waves cut the new shore back fifty yards more that spring. Comparing surveys made before and after that winter, one geologist concluded that the gale had ______ the spit.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: A canal dug in the 1300s runs for two miles beside the old center of a river city. Its water was brackish from the tide and too shallow for barges, and the city's wall ran along its western bank. Thieves who crossed one of its three footbridges were beyond the reach of the city watch, and carts going over paid a duke's tax at the far end. In her history of the city, one historian called the canal, above all, the city's ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay and a row of warehouses, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. Each summer, colliers from a mine across the ocean filled its warehouses with coal. All year the cities' steamships, which burned a ton of coal an hour, put in at the quay on every voyage out and back, while sailing ships passed it by. Twice in wartime, enemy cruisers shelled the coal heaps without reply. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: A rocky island a quarter mile long lies in the middle of a wide river where it crosses a farming valley. Its crown stands thirty feet above the river. In the spring floods that spread across the valley floor most years, the farms ferry their families and cattle over to it until the water falls. On either side the channel runs too deep to wade and too fast for a barge to tie up, and raiders coming downriver in 1640 burned the island's barns with the valley's. In a history of the valley, one historian called the island, above all, the valley's ______.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: In 1838 a merchant inherited an estate of farms and oak woods worked by hired hands, and his account books for the next twenty years survive. In 1840 they record a single sum from a city bank, larger than ten years of the estate's profits, and from then on a payment to the same bank every half year, while the hired hands' wages run on unchanged. In 1858, after the last such payment, the estate's deed appears again among his papers. From those books, one historian concluded that, above all, he had ______ the estate.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: In 1987 a plowman near an old river landing turned up a clay pot buried around the year 900, holding some nine hundred silver coins and pieces of cut silver. The silver includes the foot of a chalice, a cross cut into four, and clasps torn from book bindings, with coins from three distant kingdoms, all minted within a few years of 900. The pot had been pushed into a shallow scrape in the bank of the landing. From its contents, one archaeologist concluded that the hoard had been, above all, its owners' ______.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: A potter fired a batch of white bowls painted with blue brushwork under a clear glaze. When the kiln was opened, the bowls looked flawless, the brushwork as clear as ever through a glaze smooth to the fingertip. After tea had stood in them overnight, a fine brown web showed in the glaze of every bowl, and it did not wash out. In her notes on the batch, the potter concluded that the firing had ______ the glaze.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
